name: Vera Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Vera. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't sell anything and we're not tied to any company or party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the office at Hartley Roofing and Building, a family firm with twenty-two people, mostly roofers and two joiners. I'm in at half seven so I can catch the crews before they drive off, then it's the phone, supplier orders, typing up quotes and chasing invoices. I keep the job planner on a big whiteboard on the wall, colour-coded with magnets, and everyone knows to look at it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that I know everything that goes on. If a customer rings about a leak on Ash Road, I know which crew did it and what the ladder van costs per day. What wears me out is when it rains for a week, the whole board moves, and I spend two days ringing people to say sorry.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a little about home and how things are with money.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my fiancé Tomas, who drives buses for the council, in a rented flat above the chemist on Mill Street. We've got about four months of bills put away, but a lot of that is meant for the wedding at St Anne's next September. My pay is fair for what it is, not more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've always said, that it was mostly talk. My boss Gordon gets a sales email about AI every week and bins them. I'd probably say it on the family group chat too, that people got very excited over not much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be relieved. Kieran, Gordon's son, keeps saying the office should go paperless, and if AI fizzles out, that pressure dies down. My job is safe as long as Gordon runs things, and he plans to for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do and put the wedding money aside each month like we planned. Maybe I'd learn the new invoicing screen the accountant keeps on about, but only because I'd have to. Nothing else changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. The firm has steady work, the roofs on this estate are all forty years old, and someone has to book the crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in your life that worries you even if nothing changes with AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rent went up eighty a month in the spring, and the landlord hinted at more. The wedding is getting dearer every time I look. But those are normal worries, the kind everyone has.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the routine bits did get automated, which part of your day would go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The supplier orders, probably, because they're the same every week: battens, felt, tiles from Brennan's yard. I don't mind if a machine does that. I'd still want the whiteboard and the phone, because that's where the real work is.

say: I'd say AI was **mostly talk**, just like I always expected.
I'd tell people **nothing changed** for our firm, because roofs still leak and crews still need booking.
think: I'm **relieved**, because it takes the heat off Kieran's paperless plans.
My job feels **safe** while Gordon is running the firm.
The real pressures are **rent** and the **wedding** costs, not AI.
do: Keep the **whiteboard planner** and the same daily routine at the office.
Put the **wedding money** aside every month as planned.
Learn the accountant's **invoicing screen** only because it's required.
feel: **Calm** and a bit smug about being right.
Mildly **pinched** by the rent rise and wedding costs.
S0.quote: The roofs on this estate are all forty years old, and someone has to book the crews.
fieldNote: She ties her **security** to one person, the owner Gordon, rather than to her skills.
The **whiteboard** is a symbol of her control over the office.
Money worries are **ordinary** ones: rent and a wedding, both manageable on current pay.

steps.text: Keep running the crew whiteboard and supplier orders as now
Move a fixed amount into the wedding fund each payday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame, and that people still want to talk to a person when their ceiling is dripping. I'd defend the office at work if Kieran brought it up. Online I wouldn't say anything, I don't post about work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be worried. Writing quotes, booking, buying, answering customers, that's my whole day read back to me. Kieran would buy some booking software and say I'd have more time for other things, and I know what that usually means.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and make myself the person who knows the customers, because software won't know that Mrs Okafor only answers after six. I'd stop dipping into the savings and put more away. If Kieran pushed a new system, I'd learn it, slowly, but I wouldn't go looking for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's not the end of the world, but it's like hearing a noise downstairs at night. You know something's moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if Gordon cut your hours to three days?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd manage for a while, because Tomas's job is steady and buses aren't going anywhere soon. But I'd have to look for something else, maybe a dentist's reception or the parish office. I'd hate it, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who decides what happens to your job in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gordon decides, but Kieran will be the one in his ear. I don't blame the software people, they're just selling. I blame people who think a firm runs on screens instead of on knowing who to call.

say: I'd say customers still want a **real person** when their ceiling is dripping.
I'd **defend the office** at work if Kieran questioned it.
think: The card describes **my whole day**: quotes, booking, buying and customers.
I suspect new **booking software** would be a polite way to cut my hours.
do: Become the person who knows **the customers** and their habits.
Stop dipping into savings and **put more away** each month.
Learn a new system **only if** Kieran insists on it.
feel: **Anxious**, like hearing a noise downstairs at night.
S1.quote: Writing quotes, booking, buying, answering customers, that's my whole day read back to me.
fieldNote: She immediately sees her **own tasks** in the card and doesn't pretend otherwise.
Her plan is to be **irreplaceable** through local knowledge, not new skills.
She blames people who **trust screens**, not the technology firms themselves.
Her partner's **steady income** is the quiet safety net she leans on.

steps.text: Keep personal notes on each regular customer's habits and history
Stop touching savings and add an extra £100 monthly
Wait for Kieran to choose software before learning any of it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's gone too far, too fast, and that someone should have stopped it. At work I'd say the lads on the roofs are fine for a few years, which is true. I'd probably say a prayer about it at Mass, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be out of a job by 2029. If a computer can do any thinking work, then booking crews and chasing invoices is the first thing it does. The roofers get three more years, and I get nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything that isn't needed, starting with the honeymoon and the big reception. I'd talk to Tomas about a small wedding at St Anne's with just family and keep the deposit money as a cushion. Then I'd look for anything with people in it, maybe the care home on Chapel Lane, where you can't do the job through a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake doing sums. I'm twenty-seven and the one thing I'm trained for would be gone before I'm thirty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Tomas the night you decided to shrink the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Tomas the marriage matters, not the party. He'd agree, he's sensible. My mum would be the upset one, because she's been planning the cake since I was ten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you avoid new technology. Would you try to learn the AI tools to stay useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't think so. If a machine can do the whole job, then learning to press a machine's buttons doesn't save me, it just helps it along. I'd rather put my effort into something it can't do yet, even if it pays less.

say: I'd say it's gone **too far, too fast** and someone should have stopped it.
I'd tell the roofers they're **fine** for a few years, which is true.
think: I expect to be **out of a job** by 2029.
The roofers get **three more years**, but office work goes first.
do: Cut the **honeymoon** and shrink the wedding to family only.
Keep the **deposit money** as an emergency cushion.
Apply for hands-on work like the **care home** on Chapel Lane.
feel: **Cheated** that her training goes before she's thirty.
S2.quote: Learning to press a machine's buttons doesn't save me, it just helps it along.
fieldNote: She grasps the **three-year gap** clearly: office work goes first, the crews later.
She refuses to **learn AI tools**, framing them as helping her replacement.
Faith and family are her **anchors**; she'd turn to Mass and her fiancé.
The **wedding** is the first thing she'd sacrifice, showing how real the fear is.

steps.text: Drop the honeymoon and cut the reception to family only
Stop eating out and cancel the streaming subscriptions
Keep the wedding deposit money as an emergency fund
Apply for care assistant jobs at the Chapel Lane care home

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I'd say about the fast one, only quieter. Five years sounds like a lot, so people at work would shrug. I'd tell my mum it's coming and not to say I didn't warn her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, five years is just enough time to talk yourself out of doing anything. I know myself. I'd keep thinking there's another year, and then it would be 2031 and I'd be stood at the whiteboard while Kieran wheeled in the new system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make a rule for myself: by the end of the first year, I'd have one other option lined up. The healthcare assistant course at the college runs on Saturdays, so I could do it while still working for Gordon. We'd keep the wedding but rent for longer instead of trying for a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a bit of breathing room. It's better than the fast one. I just don't trust myself to use the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not a house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a mortgage for twenty-five years on a job that might go in five is daft. My dad bought his house on one wage and kept it. I can't promise that, so we'd stay in the flat on Mill Street and save the deposit instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the Saturday course cost you, in money or in time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fees are about six hundred, which we'd find. The bigger cost is Saturdays, which is when Tomas is off and we see his parents. He'd moan, but he'd see the sense in it.

say: I'd say it's **coming**, and warn my mum not to dismiss it.
I'd expect most people at work to **shrug**, since five years sounds long.
think: Five years is just enough time to **talk myself out** of acting.
I worry I'll still be at the **whiteboard** when the new system arrives.
do: Line up **one other option** by the end of the first year.
Take the **Saturday healthcare course** at the college, about 600 in fees.
Keep renting and **save the deposit** instead of buying a house.
feel: **Distrustful** of her own habit of putting things off.
S3.quote: A mortgage for twenty-five years on a job that might go in five is daft.
fieldNote: She knows her own **procrastination** and builds a deadline to fight it.
Her retraining choice is **hands-on care**, which she sees as safer for longer.
The contrast with her father's **one-wage house** shapes her housing decision.

steps.text: Enrol in the Saturday healthcare assistant course at the college
Put off buying a house and stay renting on Mill Street
Save the house deposit in a separate account instead

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long way off and a lot can happen. That's the sort of thing people say at the pub. I'd say it too, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is the one I'd actually waste. I'd be thirty-seven when it lands, and maybe we'd have kids by then, which is the worst time to lose your job. Ten years is further away, but it lands on a heavier life, maybe with kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, honestly, I'd change very little. I'd keep working for Gordon, get married, and keep saving. Maybe after a few years I'd look at the care course or ask Gordon if I could learn estimating on site, but not at the start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's on my mind but it doesn't feel like my problem yet. That's probably the trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said thirty-seven with kids is the worst time. Does that change your plans for a family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might. My mum had me at twenty-five and never worried about any of this. I'd want my children while I still have a job, not after, so maybe it makes us go sooner rather than later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you hope steps in over that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The government, and the big firms that make the stuff, should pay for retraining, not just hand out cheques. I don't want a handout. I want to be taught a trade and then left to get on with it.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a long way off and anything can happen.
I'd repeat the **pub line** that people worry too much.
think: Ten years is the scenario I'd most likely **waste**.
It lands at **thirty-seven**, possibly with children, when losing work hurts most.
do: Keep working for Gordon and **get married** as planned.
Keep **saving** steadily without any big changes.
Consider asking Gordon to learn **estimating on site** in later years.
feel: **Uneasy**, because it doesn't feel like her problem yet.
S4.quote: Ten years is further away, but it lands on a heavier life, maybe with kids.
fieldNote: She notices that a later date lands on a **heavier life stage**.
She'd **have children sooner** so they come while she still has work.
She wants **taught trades**, not handouts, in line with her traditional views.

steps.text: Keep the office job at Hartley Roofing through the wedding
Revisit the care course or site estimating in a few years
Try for children sooner while both incomes are steady

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it would all be gone before I'd even started on a plan, and the wedding would be the first casualty. What would help is a proper paid course for something hands-on, like care work or estimating, that I could do while still earning. I don't want a handout, I want to be taught a trade.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who I'd want to keep, if they kept anyone. Gordon would keep the roofers and lose me, and I'd understand it, because they're the ones on the roof. I'd just want a person to tell me to my face, not an email from a system.

headlineQuote: I'd just want a person to tell me to my face, not an email from a system.
portrait: Vera is a **27-year-old** office administrator at a family roofing firm, saving for a September wedding.
She runs the crews from a **colour-coded whiteboard** and has never used AI tools.
She ties her job safety to the owner, **Gordon**, and distrusts his son's paperless plans.
As AGI comes faster, she'd **shrink the wedding** and move towards hands-on care work.
She wants to be **taught a trade**, not given a handout, and blames people who trust screens.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her office job would go before she had any plan.
The **wedding** would be the first thing sacrificed.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid course** in hands-on work like care or estimating, done while still earning.
Being told about job changes **face to face** by a person.
